UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


American Transmission Company L.L.C.                          )
Amended Large Load Project Commitment                         )                     Docket No. ER26-3265-000
and Minimum Transmission Charge Assessment                    )


                            MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
                      AND ANSWER OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”

or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Data Center Coalition (“DCC”)2 respectfully submit

this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the comments, protests and answers filed in the

captioned proceeding by American Transmission Company LLC, by its corporate manager, ATC

Management Inc. (collectively, “ATC” as the Transmission Owner), Wisconsin Electric Power

Company (“WEPCo”), the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin (“CUB”), the Wisconsin Industrial

Energy Group (“WIEG”) and Microsoft Corporation (“Microsoft”). 3 Despite ATC’s and

WEPCo’s assertions to the contrary, the proposed four Amended Large Load Project Commitment

Agreements (“Amended LLPCAs”) and the Minimum Transmission Charge Agreement

(“MTCA”) (collectively, the “Agreements”) between ATC and WEPCo (the “Parties”), dated July

24, 2026,4 fail to satisfy the Federal Power Act’s (“FPA”) Section 205 requirement that they be

 just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory. The Agreements also fail to comply with both the

Commission’s June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause (“Show Cause Order”), 5 as well as the

Commission’s allowance of a 90-day Abeyance to meet the requirements of the Show Cause

Order.6

       I.      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

            Although the Commission’s procedural rules do not generally allow answers to comments,

protests, or answers, the Commission may permit them for good cause. 7 The Commission

frequently accepts answers that clarify the issues before the Commission, ensure a complete

record, or otherwise assist the Commission in its decision-making. 8 DCC respectfully requests

that the Commission accept this answer as it will facilitate the Commission’s decisional process

and clarify certain issues in this proceeding, including DCC’s positions as filed in its Comments

and Limited Protest.9

     II.       BACKGROUND

            On July 24, 2026, ATC filed the Agreements between itself and WEPCo in this proceeding

stating, in part, that the Agreements were for a large load customer – namely, Microsoft’s new

data center in Racine County, Wisconsin. ATC also averred that the Agreements were “responsive

or a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”).

information that assisted the Commission’s decision making process); Alaska Gasline Development Corp., 171 FERC
¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting answers that “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted

 to the Commission’s recent Order to Show Cause on large loads.” 10 In citing the Show Cause

Order, ATC noted in a footnote that:

                The Commission specifically invited Transmission Owners, such as ATC,
                to respond to the Order to Show Cause in an ‘FPA section 205 filing, to
                submit original proposals designed to address the concerns expressed herein
                and tailored to their unique circumstances.’ Id. at P 116. The Amended
                LLPCAs and MTCA has been developed to address the Commission’s
                concerns in a manner specifically tailored to ATC’s unique circumstance as
                a transmission only company and to adequately protect ATC’s other
                wholesale customers while supporting WEPCo’s efforts to provide
                protections at the retail-level.11

ATC also stated that the “protections provided by the Amended LLPCAs and MTCA are directly

responsive to the Commission’s recent Order to Show Cause related to large load

interconnections.”12 ATC cited numerous other examples of how the Agreements are “guided by

the Order to Show Cause”13 and are allegedly “compliant with the Commission’s Show Cause

Order, citing, in part, how ATC and WEPCo “have collaboratively developed appropriate

mechanisms to address the Commission’s concerns by ensuring costs are allocated in a just and

reasonable manner at the wholesale level.”14

       In ATC’s Answer, ATC states, in part, that the “broader policy issues discussed in the

Commission’s Show Cause Order raised here by the [Public Service Commission of Wisconsin]

and other intervenors are beyond the scope of ATC’s current filing. Nothing in this filing is

intended to serve as a pro forma agreement and ATC’s compliance with the Show Cause Order is

currently before the Commission in Docket No. ER26-3531.” 15 ATC references the “current

 version” of the LLPCA and MTCA that ATC filed as a revision to its current local planning process

in Attachment FF-ATCLLC in Docket No. ER26-3531, and which ATC proposes to use for future

large load requests. These Agreements in Docket No. ER26-3531 are also not pro forma

agreements but rather are intended as the model for further “templates” for large load agreements

that ATC will file “on a case by case basis for acceptance with the Commission.” 16

    III.        ANSWER

                A. ATC Has Not Met Its Burden of Proof Under FPA Section 205
           Pursuant to the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) Section 205, the filing public utility proposing

tariff revisions bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that its proposal is just, reasonable, and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential.17 The Commission will not resolve evidentiary gaps in

a proposal in order to develop the substantial evidence that would be required to accept a proposal

that was inadequately supported when filed.18 Rather, the Commission routinely rejects Section

205 filings when the filing utility fails to meet its burden of proof. 19 It is most critical that the

Commission do so here, as the Agreements raise substantial and fundamental questions of unjust

and unreasonable rates, discriminatory service amongst similarly-situated end-use customers, and

may prove detrimental to the Commission’s goal of creating timely, clear and transparent tariff




           16
             Id. p. 17.
           17
             16 U.S.C. § 824d.
          18
             See Sw. Power Pool, Inc. GridLiance High Plains LLC, 180 FERC ¶ 61,192 at P 52 (2022) (“The party
with the burden of proof bears the burden of production, or the need to provide sufficient evidence to establish a prima
facie case”); see also, e.g., Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1342, 1351 (4th Cir. 1984) (“Nantahala”)
(“A utility bears the burden of justifying each component of” a proposed rate change and “[b]ecause a regulated utility
is the party with access to the necessary information, it bears the risk of an undeveloped or inconclusive record”); Nw.
Corp. v. FERC, 884 F.3d 1176, 1182-83 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (explaining that “because it was [the utility’s] burden under
Section 205 to show that its proposed rate was just and reasonable, [] failure [to do so] was fatal” and rejecting
arguments that it was FERC’s burden to identify alternative bases for finding the proposed rate just and reasonable).
          19
             Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 191 FERC ¶ 61,131 at P 197 (2025) (rejecting tariff
revisions where filer failed to meet Section 205 burden show approach for addressing resource adequacy and reliability
needs was just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential).

                                                           4
 provisions sufficient to safeguard all ratepayers while stimulating the crucial development of large

loads.

         At its core, the Agreements raise substantial cost allocation issues that cannot be adequately

resolved without further stakeholder hearings or settlement proceedings. Despite ATC’s

attestations that the Agreements appropriately address cost-of-service and any cost shifting

amongst its customers the specified new large load, DCC agrees with the concerns raised by other

parties that the Agreements may result in unjust and unreasonable rates for transmission service

for numerous reasons.

         As WIEG notes, no cost-of-service studies were included in ATC’s July 24 Filings. 20 Some

of the many factual cost issues raised are that the Agreements: do not appropriately mitigate the

risk of cost shifting between ATC’s transmission customers; 21 may lead to overcharging or

undercharging of costs with no opportunity for correction; are not based on the costs of the

incremental facilities constructed to serve the new large load; may result in large load customers

paying twice; will invariably lock in over- and under-charges to WEPCo’s large load customers;

include an early termination fee that is unsupported by the record and inconsistent with cost-of-

service ratemaking; and include a legally questionable Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”)

rate, amongst other issues.22

         The issue of cost causation is one of the fundamental principles of just and reasonable rates,

requiring that rates be aligned with the benefits received and costs imposed by customers,




         20
            WIEG Comments, p. 3.
         21
            CUB Comments/Lmt. Protest, at p. 1; 3-5.
         22
            Microsoft Protest, pp. 5-26.

                                                       5
 consistent with the “just and reasonable” standard of the Federal Power Act. 23 While ATC agrees

to correct one cost provision error and to make a revision in a later compliance filing to address

another cost issue,24 ATC otherwise disputes all of the other cost allocation issues and concerns.

Notably, these cost allocation issues are all raised by customers (representing residential, industrial

and large load) that have had no stakeholder involvement in the creation of these important large

load agreements.

         The fact that ATC disputes these cost allocation issues does not mean that they cease to be

factual issues. Quite the opposite. They demonstrate that the record before the Commission is

incomplete and that the Agreements do not contain cost allocation measures that have been

demonstrated to be “just and reasonable.”

         Furthermore, contrary to the claims by ATC and WEPCo, no party to this proceeding is

requesting that the Commission choose a different or alternative cost allocation agreement. Rather,

parties have raised valid issues and concerns that indicate that ATC’s and WEPCo’s proposed

Agreements are not “reasonable” ones. 25

         Finally, while it is true that DCC does not seek to disturb specified commercial

arrangements for a project under development, 26 that is only true to the extent that they remain

limited bilateral commercial arrangements that do not purport to establish a precedent to be

(“Under the Act, electric utilities must charge ‘just and reasonable’ rates. For decades, the Commission and the courts
have understood this requirement to incorporate a ‘cost-causation principle’ – that the rates charged for electricity
should reflect the costs of providing it.”
         24

Microsoft proposes.
         25
            WEPCo Answer, p. 3, footnote 8, citing Entergy Svcs., Inc. v. FERC, 40 F.4th 689, 701–02 (D.C. Cir.
2022) (finding that the Commission is not required to choose the best solution, only a reasonable one.)
         26
            Comments and Limited Protest of Data Center Coalition, ER26-3265, dated, pp. 5-6.

                                                          6
 followed in the future. DCC has been clear that the Agreements in this proceeding are not pro

forma agreements and should not be treated as such. Yet ATC indicates in its Answer that

essentially “updated” versions of these Agreements will, in fact, operate as “template” agreements

to be filed for future large load developments on a “case by case basis.” 27 ATC cannot have it

both ways. It must either seek Commission approval for a limited bilaterial commercial

arrangement (in which case it may not treat that arrangement as if it were pro forma), or it must

openly propose a pro forma agreement and submit to the level of scrutiny and stakeholder input

required for pro forma arrangements.

              B. The Agreements Are Presented As Complying With The Commission’s Show
                 Cause Order But They Categorically Do Not

       DCC agrees with WIEG’s observation that despite ATC’s statements in its July 24 Filing

wherein it “expressly asserts” that the Agreements comply with the Commission’s Show Cause

Order, “it is highly questionable whether ATC’s proposed localized, contract-based approach fully

comports with the Commission’s overarching directives.” 28 The Commission should affirmatively

find that they do not. ATC is attempting to have it both ways in its use of the Show Cause Order

to support these Agreements. On the one hand, ATC acknowledges that these Agreement are not

pro forma agreements. But it still attests in every other way that the Agreements are in response

to - and in compliance with - the Commission’s Show Cause Order. And simultaneously, ATC

wants to claim in its Answer that issues relating to the Show Cause Order are “beyond the scope”

of this proceeding and are better addressed in the ER26-3531 proceeding where substantially

similar but “updated” Agreements have been filed. The Commission should see through such

procedural gamesmanship.


       27
            ATC Answer, p. 17.
       28
            WIEG Comments/Protest, p. 4.

                                                7
         The fact that they are not pro forma agreements means that they lack the requisite

standardization, transparency and certainty that would alleviate the real possibility of

discriminatory treatment amongst similarly situated end use customers. DCC agrees with WIEG’s

concern that the Agreements amount to a “piecemeal, decentralized approach” that “creates

regulatory uncertainty and a highly fragmented landscape” to address transmission cost allocation

for large loads.29

        The Commission granted MISO’s and the Transmission Owner’s (including ATC’s)

request for a 90-day Abeyance of the Show Cause Order for the very reason that many of the issues

connected with new tariff provisions to address the large loads are complicated and need the focus

and dedication of all affected stakeholders working towards future FPA Section 205 filings that

are, in fact, just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory. ATC and WEPCo obtained such a

grant of an Abeyance and yet have filed these Agreements with no interested party or stakeholder

input whatsoever. This is contrary to the Commission’s Order granting the Abeyance Request.

Specifically, the Commission found, in part, that:

                   We grant the Abeyance Motion filed by MISO and the MISO TOs.
                   Consistent with the Show Cause Order, MISO and the MISO TOs have
                   provided a description of the filings MISO anticipates making, provided
                   dates by which MISO intends to make such filings, and described the on-
                   going stakeholder process, including stakeholder meeting dates. Such a
                   stakeholder process will provide MISO, the Transmission Owners, and
                   other stakeholders an opportunity to consider region-specific solutions to
                   the concerns raised in the Show Cause Order. MISO states that it intends
                   to submit a series of FPA section 205 filings during the abeyance period,
                   with the first filing by the end of August. 30

ATC’s and WEPCo’s Agreements not only failed to have any stakeholder process, they also fail

to address large load cost allocation issues on a regional basis, instead opting for one-off large load


        29
             Ibid.
        30
             Abeyance Order, p. 6, P 8 (emphasis added).

                                                           8
 costing requirements that can be discriminatorily and unilaterally tailored by ATC and WEPCo.

Both are contrary to the Commission’s Abeyance Order and the FPA Section 205’s requirement

that wholesale rates not be unduly discriminatory or preferential.


          DCC believes that while a Transmission Owner has the right to file individual cost recovery

agreements, the Commission’s goal and intent of the Show Cause Order was, in part, the creation

of “a pro forma cost recovery agreement between MISO, the relevant transmission owner, and the

Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf of a large load, or to propose Tariff

revisions to provide additional transparency and establish such a pro forma cost recovery

agreement.”31 DCC continues to believe that these Agreements do not satisfy these requirements.

          ATC and WEPCo should not be allowed to do an end-run around the Commission’s Show

Cause Order by seeking approval of new, large load cost agreements that will be used as large load

cost recovery “templates” until the creation of pro forma cost agreements with MISO and

stakeholders. Therefore, DCC respectfully requests that the Commission agree with Microsoft’s

request for hearing and settlement judge procedures for the Agreements in this proceeding, or,

alternatively, that the Commission dismiss ATC’s July 24 Filing without prejudice in order for

ATC to work with MISO and other stakeholders to make a future pro forma cost allocation filing

no earlier than the date by which MISO will make its Large Load 205 filings – i.e., November 16,

2026.

    IV.          CONCLUSION

          For the reasons stated herein, DCC respectfully requests that the Commission initiate

hearing and settlement judge procedures to allow all interested parties to resolve the deficiencies

               Show Cause Order, pp. 43-44, P 67.

                                                    9
 described in this proceeding. In the alternative, DCC respectfully requests that the Commission

reject the Agreements without prejudice so that they may be worked on through MISO’s Large

Load Working Group stakeholder process.
